title: Love at first bite: The Paltok bakery that sells out early
summary: Residents of Paltok, Quezon City, flock to a yellow-walled corner bakery every day before its freshly baked bread sells out

blocks.text: Carmen Mariano, 65, used to wonder why so little bread remained whenever she passed by the small bakery in her neighborhood in Barangay Paltok, Quezon City.

It’s called Bong & Dynah Bakeshop, but residents have taken to calling it Matias Bakery, a nod to the street where it’s located. The small shop opens at 5 am to serve classic baked goods to early risers, and for the longest time, Carmen thought the bakery simply offered an oddly tiny selection of bread.
“Anong klaseng bakery ba ‘to? (What kind of bakery is this?)” Carmen would often say to herself whenever she laid her eyes on the big glass case situated in front of the store.
It turned out, however, that by the time she would arrive at the bakeshop, most of them had just already been bought by other customers who happened to get there before she did.
Carmen is now a regular at the bakeshop — making the trip for buns, banana cake, and egg pie. Her son also buys pandesal in the morning.

When Bong & Dynah Bakeshop opens its doors at the crack of dawn, its staff only has a window of one to two hours to enjoy the lull before the morning rush starts. Hordes of customers start pouring in by 6 or 7 am, and by 8 or 9 am, its pandesal is completely sold out.
Spanish bread and pan de coco are among the bakery’s bestsellers, said Dynah Carizal, who owns the shop with her husband Cornellio “Bong” Carizal.

blocks.caption: Spanish bread, pan de coco, and pastries at Bong & Dynah Bakeshop.

blocks.text: This is already Dynah’s second bakery. After spending 10 years as a call center agent, she saved up enough to try her hand at a pastry business again with Bong. Now, the shop is a year old and counting.
The space used to house tapsilog, lugaw, pancit, and fried chicken businesses, until it turned itself into a yellow-walled bakery that residents have quickly come to love.
Bong said their immediate goal is to keep serving customers and keep the business afloat.
“Kami, kumbaga, dahan-dahan lang. Basta magsurvive tayo,” he said.
(We’re taking it slowly. We just want to survive.)

More than just survival, Bong & Dynah Bakeshop has now become a familiar stop despite surrounding businesses coming and going. It’s a staple that looks like it’s here to stay, so long as the people of Paltok keep their love for pastries alive.

Dynah said customers often overlook the time needed for dough to rise, which takes about five to six hours to complete. Bong said that a second batch of the famous salt bread could be ready only after the morning demand dies down.

Making bread is a labor of love that takes more than just mixing ingredients and sticking the dough in the oven. This is something baker Genesis Ordano, who has been working at the shop for 16 years, knows full well.

blocks.caption: Empty shelves show the sold-out putok/star bread. The shop also offers toasted siopao for P15.

blocks.text: Genesis said getting the mixture right takes work customers rarely see. Production uses two and a half sacks of flour, rising to three when sales are good. Like clockwork, the longtime baker — who attests that nothing about the practice of baking challenges him — can recite the whole process of preparing pandesal off the top of his head.
“Magtitimbang muna ng asukal, tapos lalagyan ng asin at mantika. Tapos hahaluin at paalsahin muna. Tapos puputulin,” he explained.
(You weigh the sugar first, then you add salt and oil. Then, you mix it all and let it rise. Then, you cut the dough up.)

Some bread, however, sometimes goes unsold. Still, nothing goes to waste at Bong & Dynah Bakeshop. Genesis said leftovers become crumbs for pudding and custard, while Bong himself also turns some into toast with butter and sugar.

blocks.caption: P50 custard cakes made from leftover bread.

blocks.text: Bong attests that it’s the workers that keep the bakery alive.

While the bakers keep the pastries flowing, saleswoman Joanne keeps the shop running in her own way. Once she clocks in at 6:30 am, she immediately cleans the racks and sweeps up the entire space. Then, she arranges the trays and sets up the tongs and plastic bags used to pack the bread customers will buy.
Joanne, though, has a more difficult task that onlookers may not usually see.

When the demand at the bakery gets high, the challenge of keeping up with it doesn’t only depend on the bakers. It’s a burden Joanne has to bear, too. Sometimes, customers get upset when certain products sell out, but she gets through it all with patience.
“[Kailangan] habaan talaga ang pasensya. Kahit galit ka na, nakangiti ka rin,” she said.
(You really have to be patient. Even when you’re already angry, you still have to smile.)

But at the end of the day, the famed Paltok bakery turns into a home for its employees, many of whom hail from provinces like Iloilo. It provides workers with food and accommodation, and often celebrates their birthdays with meals at places like Mang Inasal.
Shelves may empty by mid-morning, but keeping the bakery going starts before its doors open.

Beyond the loyal customers who buy out the bakery’s bread every single day, the staff is a big contributor to Bong & Dynah Bakeshop’s success, even though the shop is only a year old. Perhaps Bong and Dynah, then, have found the formula to fulfilling their dream of making the bakery survive. – Rappler.com
Jade Tan is a Rappler intern studying AB Journalism at University of Santo Tomas, Manila.
